items.edition: Specimens of the Classic Poets, in a Chronological Series from Homer to Tryphiodorus, translated into English verse, vol. I (London: Robert Baldwin, 1814)
items.citation: Archilochus, "Exhortation to Fortitude, under Calamity", Elton, Specimens I p. 87
items.text:
Groans rise on griefs, oh Pericles! nor they
Who feed the woe, in wine or feast are gay.
The billow of the many-roaring deep
Has borne these pleasures in its whelming sweep.
Our grief-swol'n hearts, now, draw their breath in pain;
Yet blessings, oh my friend! shall smile again.
The Gods reserve for seeming-cureless woe
A balm, and antidotes on grief bestow.
In turn the cure and suffering take their round,
And we now groaning feel the bleeding wound:
Now other breasts the shifting tortures know;
Endure; nor droop thus womanish in woe.
items.coverage_note: Elton renders the whole 10-line elegy to Pericles in 12 rhymed lines; same extent as Campbell. Elton's section heading names other English translators (e.g. 'English translator: Bland') as a reference list; the specimens themselves are Elton's own versions (they differ from Bland's 1813 versions; Dole's The Greek Poets, 1904, credits them to Elton). Elton prints no Greek; match is by content.
items.match_evidence: Opens with groans/griefs addressed to Pericles, no citizen delighting in feasts (lines 1-2), the billow of the many-roaring sea (3), grief-swollen breasts (4-5), the gods giving endurance as remedy for incurable ills (5-7), the suffering turning now to us, now to others (7-9), and the closing command to thrust away womanish grief (10).

items.edition: Specimens of the Classic Poets, in a Chronological Series from Homer to Tryphiodorus, translated into English verse, vol. I (London: Robert Baldwin, 1814)
items.citation: Archilochus, "On an Eclipse of the Sun", Elton, Specimens I p. 88
items.text:
Nought, now, can pass belief; in Nature's ways
No strange anomaly our wonder raise.
Th' Olympian Father hangs a noon-day night
O'er the sun's disk, and veils its glittering light.
Fear falls on man. Hence miracles, before
Incredible, are counted strange no more.
Stand not amazed if beasts exchange the wood
With dolphins; and exist amidst the flood;
These the firm land forsake for sounding waves,
And those find pleasure in the mountain caves.
items.coverage_note: Elton's 10 lines render Campbell lines 1-9 (nothing unexpected; Zeus makes night at noon; fear; let none marvel if beasts exchange pasture with dolphins and prefer the sea, and they the mountain). Campbell's papyrus-supplemented lines 10-16 (Archenactides etc.) are not in Elton. Elton's section heading names other English translators (e.g. 'English translator: Bland') as a reference list; the specimens themselves are Elton's own versions (they differ from Bland's 1813 versions; Dole's The Greek Poets, 1904, credits them to Elton). Elton prints no Greek; match is by content.
items.match_evidence: Nothing past belief; the Olympian Father makes a noon-day night hiding the sun (Campbell 1-4); fear on men; let no one be amazed if beasts exchange their pasture with dolphins and the sea, and dolphins love the mountains (6-9).

items.edition: Specimens of the Classic Poets, in a Chronological Series from Homer to Tryphiodorus, translated into English verse, vol. I (London: Robert Baldwin, 1814)
items.citation: Archilochus, "Equanimity", Elton, Specimens I p. 88
items.text:
Spirit, thou Spirit, like a troubled sea,
Ruffled with deep and hard calamity,
Sustain the shock: a daring heart oppose:
Stand firm, amidst the charging spears of foes:
If conquering, vaunt not in vain-glorious show:
If conquer'd, stoop not, prostrated in woe:
Moderate, in joy, rejoice; in sorrow, mourn:
Muse on man's lot: be thine discreetly borne.
items.coverage_note: Elton renders the whole 7-line trochaic fragment in 8 lines; same extent as Campbell. Elton's section heading names other English translators (e.g. 'English translator: Bland') as a reference list; the specimens themselves are Elton's own versions (they differ from Bland's 1813 versions; Dole's The Greek Poets, 1904, credits them to Elton). Elton prints no Greek; match is by content.
items.match_evidence: Address to the spirit (thymos) troubled by helpless cares (Campbell 1); oppose the breast to the foe and stand firm (2-4); neither exult openly in victory nor collapse lamenting in defeat (4-5); rejoice in joys and grieve in ills moderately, and know the rhythm that holds mankind (6-7).

items.edition: Specimens of the Classic Poets, in a Chronological Series from Homer to Tryphiodorus, translated into English verse, vol. I (London: Robert Baldwin, 1814)
items.citation: Mimnermus, "Shortness of Life", Elton, Specimens I pp. 121-122
items.text:
We, like the leaves of many-blossom'd spring,
When the sun's rays their sudden radiance fling,
In growing strength, on earth, a little while,
Delighted, see youth's blooming flow'rets smile.
Not with that wisdom of the Gods endued,
To judge aright of evil and of good.
Two Fates, dark-scowling, at our side attend;
Of youth, of life, each points the destin'd end,
Old age, and death: the fruit of youth remains
Brief, as the sunshine scatter'd o'er the plains:
And, when these fleeting hours have fled away,
To die were better than to breathe the day.
A load of grief the burthen'd spirit wears;
Domestic troubles rise; penurious cares;
One with an earnest love of children sighs;
The grave is open'd, and he childless dies:
Another drags in pain his lingering days,
While slow disease upon his vitals preys.
Nor lives there one, whom Jupiter on high
Exempts from years of mix'd calamity.
items.coverage_note: Elton renders the whole 16-line elegy in 20 lines; same extent as Campbell. Elton's section heading names other English translators (e.g. 'English translator: Bland') as a reference list; the specimens themselves are Elton's own versions (they differ from Bland's 1813 versions; Dole's The Greek Poets, 1904, credits them to Elton). Elton prints no Greek; match is by content.
items.match_evidence: We are like the leaves of flowery spring growing in the sun (Campbell 1-2), enjoying youth a short while, knowing neither good nor ill from the gods (3-5); two dark Fates, old age and death (5-7); the fruit of youth brief as sunlight (7-8); better to die at once (10); troubles, poverty, childlessness, disease (11-15); no man to whom Zeus does not give many ills (15-16).

items.edition: Specimens of the Classic Poets, in a Chronological Series from Homer to Tryphiodorus, translated into English verse, vol. I (London: Robert Baldwin, 1814)
items.citation: Mimnermus, "Reproach of Old Age", Elton, Specimens I p. 123
items.text:
What joy in life, were golden Venus fled?
Then may I sleep among the silent dead,
When this can charm no more; when tasteless prove
Soft bribes, the yielding couch, clandestine love.
What joy in life, if, with such transient bloom,
Youth's dropping flow'rets waste their rich perfume,
And both the sexes droop? then age is nigh;
At whose afflictive touch the Graces fly.
The fair-proportion'd limbs of smooth delight
Deform'd, dishonour'd, loveless to the sight.
Perpetual miseries make the soul their prey;
The aged man looks up, and loathes the day:
Of boys the mock; of women the disdain;
The Gods have dealt to age the dole of pain.
items.coverage_note: Elton renders the whole 10-line elegy in 14 lines; same extent as Campbell. Elton's section heading names other English translators (e.g. 'English translator: Bland') as a reference list; the specimens themselves are Elton's own versions (they differ from Bland's 1813 versions; Dole's The Greek Poets, 1904, credits them to Elton). Elton prints no Greek; match is by content.
items.match_evidence: What life, what joy without golden Aphrodite (Campbell 1); may I die when secret love, gifts and bed no longer concern me (2-3); the flowers of youth for men and women (4-5); painful old age (5-6); cares wear the mind, no joy in the sun (7-8); hateful to boys, scorned by women (9); so grievous has God made old age (10).

items.edition: Specimens of the Classic Poets, in a Chronological Series from Homer to Tryphiodorus, translated into English verse, vol. I (London: Robert Baldwin, 1814)
items.citation: Simonides [of Amorgos], "From the Apologue on Women", Elton, Specimens I pp. 159-161
items.text:
She from the steed of wanton mane
Shall spurn all servile toil and pain;
Nor shake the sieve; nor ply the mill;
Nor sweep the floor, though dusty still;
Nor near the oven take her seat;
But loathe the ashes, smoke, and heat:
And to her husband profit naught
Unless by mere compulsion taught.
Twice, thrice, she bathes her through the day,
Washing the slightest soil away:
Perfumes with oils her every limb;
Her tresses combs in order trim;
Tress upon tress in thickening braid;
While twisted flowers her temples shade,
A goodly sight to strangers' view:
But he, that owns her, sore shall rue
The cost, I ween: unless he be
Satrap or king, and joy in luxury.
Her from an Ape the Maker sent
Man's evil mate and punishment.
Her visage foul; she walks the streets,
The laughing-stock of all she meets.
Scarce her short neck can turn; all slim,
And lank, and spare; all leg and limb;
Wretched the man, who in his breast
Is doom'd to fold this female pest!
She, like the Ape, is versed in wiles;
And tricking turns; she never smiles:
Obliges none; but ponders still
On mischief-plots, and daily ill.

Who gains the creature from the Bee,
By fortune favour'd most is he:
To her alone, with pointless sting,
Would Scandal impotently cling.
With her his May of life is long;
His days are flourishing and strong.
Beloved, her fond embrace she twines
Round him she loves: with him declines
In fading years: her race is known
For goodly forms, and fair renown.
Her decent charms her sex outshine:
Around her flits a grace divine.
She sits not pleased where women crowd,
In amorous tattle, light and loud:
With such the God mankind has blest;
With such, the wisest and the best.
items.coverage_note: PARTIAL: Elton translates only three sections of the 118-line poem: the woman from the mare (Campbell lines 57-70), the woman from the ape (71-82), and the woman from the bee (83-93). The rest (sow, vixen, bitch, earth, sea, ass, weasel, and the closing lines 94-118) is not translated. Elton prints the author as 'Simonides' within his Simonides (of Ceos) section; the apologue on women is by Semonides of Amorgos. Elton's section heading names other English translators (e.g. 'English translator: Bland') as a reference list; the specimens themselves are Elton's own versions (they differ from Bland's 1813 versions; Dole's The Greek Poets, 1904, credits them to Elton). Elton prints no Greek; match is by content.
items.match_evidence: Mare-woman shuns slavish work, will not touch mill or sieve or sweep, will not sit by the oven for the ashes, bathes twice or thrice a day, anoints herself, wears her hair combed and garlanded, a fine sight for others but an expense to her husband unless he is a tyrant or sceptred king (Campbell 57-70); ape-woman, ugliest, laughing-stock of the town, short neck, no buttocks, all limbs, versed in tricks, never laughs (71-82); bee-woman, on whom no blame settles, life flourishes, grows old loving with her husband, bears a fine and famous race, conspicuous among women, a divine grace about her, does not sit among women talking of sex; Zeus grants these as the best and wisest wives (83-93).

items.edition: Collections from the Greek Anthology, by the late Rev. Robert Bland and others; a new edition, comprising the fragments of early lyric poetry ... by J. H. Merivale (London: Longman et al. and John Murray, 1833)
items.citation: Archilochus, Merivale (1833) Archilochus II "On the Loss of his Shield"
items.text:
The foe-man glories in my shield—
I left it on the battle field;
I threw it down beside the wood,
Unscath'd by scars, unstain'd with blood.
And let him glory! Since, from death
Escap'd, I keep my forfeit breath,
I soon may find, at little cost,
As good a shield as that I've lost.
items.coverage_note: Whole 4-line elegiac fragment rendered in 8 lines; same extent as Campbell. Piece signed 'M.' in the 1833 edition edited by J. H. Merivale (his own contributions; the Advertisement assigns B. to Bland, H. to Hodgson, C. M. to Charles Merivale); Dole's The Greek Poets (1904) credits these versions to John Hermann Merivale. The bracketed number is the fragment number in the editor's Greek text (Jacobs/Liebel), not printed here.
items.match_evidence: Some (Saian) foeman glories in the shield I left beside a bush, blameless armour, unwillingly (Campbell 1-2); I saved myself (3); let it go, I will get another no worse (3-4).

items.edition: Collections from the Greek Anthology, by the late Rev. Robert Bland and others; a new edition, comprising the fragments of early lyric poetry ... by J. H. Merivale (London: Longman et al. and John Murray, 1833)
items.citation: Archilochus, Merivale (1833) Archilochus III "The Close Fight"
items.text:
Bows will not avail thee,
Darts and slings will fail thee,
When Mars tumultuous rages
On wide embattled land.
Then with faulchions clashing,
Eyes with fury flashing,
Man with man engages
In combat, hand to hand.
But most Eubœa's chiefs are known,
Marshal'd hosts of spearmen leading
To conflict whence is no receding,
To make this—war's best art—their own.
items.coverage_note: Whole 5-line fragment rendered in 12 lines; same extent as Campbell. Piece signed 'M.' in the 1833 edition edited by J. H. Merivale (his own contributions; the Advertisement assigns B. to Bland, H. to Hodgson, C. M. to Charles Merivale); Dole's The Greek Poets (1904) credits these versions to John Hermann Merivale. The bracketed number is the fragment number in the editor's Greek text (Jacobs/Liebel), not printed here.
items.match_evidence: Not many bows nor frequent slings when Ares joins battle on the plain (Campbell 1-3); the grievous work of swords (3); in this the spear-famed lords of Euboea are skilled (4-5).

items.edition: Collections from the Greek Anthology, by the late Rev. Robert Bland and others; a new edition, comprising the fragments of early lyric poetry ... by J. H. Merivale (London: Longman et al. and John Murray, 1833)
items.citation: Archilochus, Merivale (1833) Archilochus V "A Pair of Military Portraits"
items.text:
Boast me not your valiant captain,
strutting fierce with measur'd stride,
Glorying in his well-trimm'd beard, and
wavy ringlets' cluster'd pride.

Mine be he that's short of stature,
firm of foot, with curved knee;
Heart of oak in limb and feature,
and of courage bold and free.
items.coverage_note: Whole 4-line trochaic fragment rendered in two quatrains (each long line printed as two half-lines); same extent as Campbell. Piece signed 'M.' in the 1833 edition edited by J. H. Merivale (his own contributions; the Advertisement assigns B. to Bland, H. to Hodgson, C. M. to Charles Merivale); Dole's The Greek Poets (1904) credits these versions to John Hermann Merivale. The bracketed number is the fragment number in the editor's Greek text (Jacobs/Liebel), not printed here.
items.match_evidence: I do not like a tall general, straddling, proud of his curls, shaven (Campbell 1-2); give me a small one, bandy-legged to look at, firm on his feet, full of heart (3-4).

items.edition: Collections from the Greek Anthology, by the late Rev. Robert Bland and others; a new edition, comprising the fragments of early lyric poetry ... by J. H. Merivale (London: Longman et al. and John Murray, 1833)
items.citation: Archilochus, Merivale (1833) Archilochus VI "Riches and Power"
items.text:
For Gyges' wealth let others care,
Gold is nothing to me;
Envy of another's share
Never shall undo me.

Nothing that the Gods decree
Moves my special wonder;
And as for boastful tyranny—
We're too far asunder.
items.coverage_note: Whole 4-line iambic fragment rendered in 8 lines; same extent as Campbell (Campbell prints it as the words of Charon the carpenter; Merivale gives no speaker). Piece signed 'M.' in the 1833 edition edited by J. H. Merivale (his own contributions; the Advertisement assigns B. to Bland, H. to Hodgson, C. M. to Charles Merivale); Dole's The Greek Poets (1904) credits these versions to John Hermann Merivale. The bracketed number is the fragment number in the editor's Greek text (Jacobs/Liebel), not printed here.
items.match_evidence: The wealth of Gyges rich in gold is no concern of mine, nor has envy seized me (Campbell 1-2); I do not marvel at the deeds of the gods (2-3); I have no love for great tyranny, it is far from my eyes (3-4).

items.edition: Collections from the Greek Anthology, by the late Rev. Robert Bland and others; a new edition, comprising the fragments of early lyric poetry ... by J. H. Merivale (London: Longman et al. and John Murray, 1833)
items.citation: Archilochus, Merivale (1833) Archilochus VIII "The Storm"
items.text:
Behold, my Glaucus! how the deep
Heaves, while the sweeping billows howl,
And round the promontory steep
The big black clouds portentous scowl,
With thunder fraught and lightning's glare,
While Terror rules, and wild Despair.
items.coverage_note: Whole 3-line trochaic fragment rendered in 6 lines; same extent as Campbell. Piece signed 'M.' in the 1833 edition edited by J. H. Merivale (his own contributions; the Advertisement assigns B. to Bland, H. to Hodgson, C. M. to Charles Merivale); Dole's The Greek Poets (1904) credits these versions to John Hermann Merivale. The bracketed number is the fragment number in the editor's Greek text (Jacobs/Liebel), not printed here.
items.match_evidence: Glaucus, look: the deep sea is troubled with waves (Campbell 1-2); a cloud stands upright round the heights of Gyrae, sign of storm (2-3); fear comes unexpectedly (3).

items.edition: Collections from the Greek Anthology, by the late Rev. Robert Bland and others; a new edition, comprising the fragments of early lyric poetry ... by J. H. Merivale (London: Longman et al. and John Murray, 1833)
items.citation: Archilochus, Merivale (1833) Archilochus IX "Moral", second part (fr. 15)
items.text:
Leave the gods to order all things:
often from the gulf of woe
They exalt the poor man grov'ling
in the gloomy shades below;
Often turn again, and prostrate
lay in dust the loftiest head,
Dooming him thro' life to wander,
reft of sense, and wanting bread.
items.coverage_note: Merivale's piece IX joins two fragments (14 = Campbell 67a, 15 = Campbell 58), separated by a printed rule; only the part after the rule (fragment 15) is given here. It renders Campbell's 5 lines. Piece signed 'M.' in the 1833 edition edited by J. H. Merivale (his own contributions; the Advertisement assigns B. to Bland, H. to Hodgson, C. M. to Charles Merivale); Dole's The Greek Poets (1904) credits these versions to John Hermann Merivale. The bracketed number is the fragment number in the editor's Greek text (Jacobs/Liebel), not printed here.
items.match_evidence: Leave all to the gods (Campbell 1); often they raise men lying on the black earth out of misfortune (1-2), often overturn those who stand firm and lay them on their backs (3-4); then many ills come, and a man wanders in want of livelihood, distraught in mind (4-5).

items.edition: Collections from the Greek Anthology, by the late Rev. Robert Bland and others; a new edition, comprising the fragments of early lyric poetry ... by J. H. Merivale (London: Longman et al. and John Murray, 1833)
items.citation: Archilochus, Merivale (1833) Archilochus XI "On Life and Death", lines 3-6 (fr. 18)
items.text:
Death seals the fountains of reward and fame:
Man dies, and leaves no guardian of his name.
Applause awaits us only while we live,
While we can honour take, and honour give:
items.coverage_note: Merivale's piece XI joins three fragments (17, 18, 19); only its lines 3-6, which render Campbell 64 (Bergk/Liebel fr. 18), are given here. Lines 1-2 render a different fragment and lines 7-8 render Campbell 65. Piece signed 'M.' in the 1833 edition edited by J. H. Merivale (his own contributions; the Advertisement assigns B. to Bland, H. to Hodgson, C. M. to Charles Merivale); Dole's The Greek Poets (1904) credits these versions to John Hermann Merivale. The bracketed number is the fragment number in the editor's Greek text (Jacobs/Liebel), not printed here.
items.match_evidence: No one, once dead, is respected or famous among the citizens (Campbell 1-2) = "Death seals the fountains of reward and fame: Man dies, and leaves no guardian of his name"; we the living pursue the favour of the living (2-3) = "Applause awaits us only while we live ...".

items.edition: Collections from the Greek Anthology, by the late Rev. Robert Bland and others; a new edition, comprising the fragments of early lyric poetry ... by J. H. Merivale (London: Longman et al. and John Murray, 1833)
items.citation: Archilochus, Merivale (1833) Archilochus XII "The Island Thasos"
items.text:
Like the sharp back-bone of an ass it stood,
That rugged Isle, o'ergrown with shaggy wood.
No verdant grot, no lawn for poet's dream,
Is there, like those by Siris' pleasant stream.
items.coverage_note: Merivale joins the two parts (21, 22) of Campbell's fragment (which marks a gap between them) without marking the gap; same extent otherwise. Piece signed 'M.' in the 1833 edition edited by J. H. Merivale (his own contributions; the Advertisement assigns B. to Bland, H. to Hodgson, C. M. to Charles Merivale); Dole's The Greek Poets (1904) credits these versions to John Hermann Merivale. The bracketed number is the fragment number in the editor's Greek text (Jacobs/Liebel), not printed here.
items.match_evidence: This island stands like the back of an ass, crowned with wild wood (Campbell 1-2); for it is no fair place nor lovely, like that about the streams of Siris (4-5).

items.edition: The Deipnosophists, or Banquet of the Learned, of Athenaeus, literally translated by C. D. Yonge, vol. III (London: Henry G. Bohn, 1854; Bohn's Classical Library)
items.citation: Archilochus quoted by Athenaeus 14.627c; Yonge, Deipnosophists III p. 1000
items.text:
But I'm a willing servant of great Mars,
Skill'd also in the Muses' lovely art.
items.coverage_note: Both lines of the fragment; same extent as Campbell. Verse rendering embedded in Yonge's translation of Athenaeus (Bohn, 1854); the surrounding prose (Athenaeus' context) is excluded. Yonge prints no Greek; match is by Athenaeus' citation and content.
items.match_evidence: I am the servant of lord Enyalius (= Mars) and skilled in the lovely gift of the Muses (Campbell 1-2).

items.edition: The Deipnosophists, or Banquet of the Learned, of Athenaeus, literally translated by C. D. Yonge, vol. I (London: Henry G. Bohn, 1854; Bohn's Classical Library)
items.citation: Archilochus quoted by Athenaeus 1.30f; Yonge, Deipnosophists I p. 51
items.text:
My spear finds corn, my spear finds wine,
From Ismarus; on my spear I dine,
And on it, when fatigued, recline.
items.coverage_note: Whole 2-line fragment rendered in 3 lines; same extent as Campbell. Verse rendering embedded in Yonge's translation of Athenaeus (Bohn, 1854); the surrounding prose (Athenaeus' context) is excluded. Yonge prints no Greek; match is by Athenaeus' citation and content.
items.match_evidence: In my spear is my kneaded bread, in my spear Ismarian wine, and I drink leaning on my spear (Campbell 1-2).

items.edition: The Deipnosophists, or Banquet of the Learned, of Athenaeus, literally translated by C. D. Yonge, vol. II (London: Henry G. Bohn, 1854; Bohn's Classical Library)
items.citation: Archilochus quoted by Athenaeus 11.483d; Yonge, Deipnosophists II p. 772
items.coverage_note: Whole 4-line elegiac fragment rendered in 6 lines; same extent as Campbell. Verse rendering embedded in Yonge's translation of Athenaeus (Bohn, 1854); the surrounding prose (Athenaeus' context) is excluded. Yonge prints no Greek; match is by Athenaeus' citation and content.
items.match_evidence: Come, go with the cup (kothon) through the benches of the swift ship (Campbell 1-2), pull the lids off the hollow casks (2), draw the red wine from the lees (3); we cannot stay sober on this watch (3-4).

items.edition: The Deipnosophists, or Banquet of the Learned, of Athenaeus, literally translated by C. D. Yonge, vol. I (London: Henry G. Bohn, 1854; Bohn's Classical Library)
items.citation: Archilochus quoted by Athenaeus 3.76b; Yonge, Deipnosophists I p. 128
items.text:
Never mind Paros, and the figs which grow
Within that marble island, and the life
Of its seafaring islanders.
items.coverage_note: The single tetrameter line rendered in 3 lines; same extent as Campbell. Verse rendering embedded in Yonge's translation of Athenaeus (Bohn, 1854); the surrounding prose (Athenaeus' context) is excluded. Yonge prints no Greek; match is by Athenaeus' citation and content.
items.match_evidence: Let Paros go, and those figs, and the seafaring life (Campbell 1).

items.edition: The Deipnosophists, or Banquet of the Learned, of Athenaeus, literally translated by C. D. Yonge, vol. III (London: Henry G. Bohn, 1854; Bohn's Classical Library)
items.citation: Archilochus quoted by Athenaeus 14.628a; Yonge, Deipnosophists III p. 1002
items.text:
I, all excited in my mind with wine,
Am skilful in the dithyrambic, knowing
The noble melodies of the sovereign Bacchus.
items.coverage_note: Both lines rendered in 3; same extent as Campbell. Verse rendering embedded in Yonge's translation of Athenaeus (Bohn, 1854); the surrounding prose (Athenaeus' context) is excluded. Yonge prints no Greek; match is by Athenaeus' citation and content.
items.match_evidence: I know how to lead off the fair song of lord Dionysus, the dithyramb, when my wits are thunderstruck with wine (Campbell 1-2).

items.edition: The Deipnosophists, or Banquet of the Learned, of Athenaeus, literally translated by C. D. Yonge, vol. II (London: Henry G. Bohn, 1854; Bohn's Classical Library)
items.citation: Mimnermus (Nanno) quoted by Athenaeus 11.470a; Yonge, Deipnosophists II pp. 748-749
items.text:
For the Sun labours every day, nor ever
Do he or his fleet steeds know pleasing rest
From that bright hour when the rosy Morn,
Leaving her ocean-bed, mounts up to heaven.
For all across the sea, a lovely bed
Of precious gold, the work of Vulcan's hands,
Conveys the god; passing on rapid wings
Along the water, while he sleeps therein,
From the bright region of th' Hesperides,
To th' Ethiopian shore, where his swift car
And fiery horses wait within their stalls
Till bright Aurora comes again and opes
Her rosy portals. Then Hyperion's son
Ascends again his swift untiring car.
items.coverage_note: Whole 11-line fragment rendered in 14 lines; same extent as Campbell. Verse rendering embedded in Yonge's translation of Athenaeus (Bohn, 1854); the surrounding prose (Athenaeus' context) is excluded. Yonge prints no Greek; match is by Athenaeus' citation and content.
items.match_evidence: The Sun's lot is toil every day, no rest for him or his horses once rosy-fingered Dawn leaves Ocean (Campbell 1-4); a lovely hollow bed, winged, of precious gold, forged by Hephaestus, carries him sleeping over the waves from the land of the Hesperides to the Ethiopians (5-9), where his chariot and horses stand until early-born Dawn comes; then Hyperion's son mounts his car (9-11).

items.edition: The Deipnosophists, or Banquet of the Learned, of Athenaeus, literally translated by C. D. Yonge, vol. III (London: Henry G. Bohn, 1854; Bohn's Classical Library)
items.citation: Hipponax (Hexameters) quoted by Athenaeus 15.698b; Yonge, Deipnosophists III p. 1116
items.text:
Muse, sing me now the praises of Eurymedon,
That great Charybdis of the sea, who holds
A sword within his stomach, never weary
With eating. Tell me how the votes may pass
Condemning him to death, by public judgment,
On the loud-sounding shore of the barren sea.
items.coverage_note: Whole 4-line hexameter parody rendered in 6 lines; same extent as Campbell (Campbell supplies ⟨κακὸς⟩ in line 3; Yonge has no equivalent word). Verse rendering embedded in Yonge's translation of Athenaeus (Bohn, 1854); the surrounding prose (Athenaeus' context) is excluded. Yonge prints no Greek; match is by Athenaeus' citation and content.
items.match_evidence: Muse, tell me of Eurymedontiades the sea-Charybdis, with a knife in his belly, who eats without order (Campbell 1-2), how he shall perish by the pebble (vote) of public decree beside the shore of the barren sea (3-4).

items.edition: The Idylls of Theocritus, Bion, and Moschus, and the War-Songs of Tyrtaeus, literally translated into English prose by the Rev. J. Banks, M.A. (London: Henry G. Bohn, 1853; Bohn's Classical Library)
items.citation: Tyrtaeus, Banks (1853), War-Songs of Tyrtaeus II
items.text: But since ye are the race of ¹invincible Hercules, be ye of good courage; not yet hath Zeus ²turned his neck aside from you. Neither fear ye, nor be affrighted at a host of men, but let hero hold his shield right against the foremost fighters; having counted life hostile, and ³the dark fates of death dear as the rays of the sun. For ye know that the ⁴works of Ares of-many-tears are much-seen, and well have ye learned the ⁵temper of troublous war. Ye have been, O young men, with the flying and the pursuing, and have pushed on to a full measure of both. Now of those, who dare, abiding one beside another, to advance to the close fray, and the foremost champions, fewer die, and they save the people in the rear; but in men ⁶that fear, all excellence is lost. No one could ever in words go through those several ills, which befall a man, ⁷if he has been actuated by cowardice. For 'tis grievous to wound in the rear the back of a flying man in hostile war. Shameful too is a corpse ⁸lying low in the dust, ⁹wounded behind in the back by the point of a spear. Rather let every one with firm stride await the enemy, having both feet fixed on the ground, biting his lip with his teeth, and having covered with the ¹⁰hollow of his broad shield thighs and shins below, and breast and shoulders. But in his right hand let him brandish a heavy lance, and ¹¹shake above his head a threatening crest. Then let him learn war, by doing bold deeds, nor let him stand with his shield out of the range of weapons. But let each, drawing nigh in close fray, ¹²hit his foe, wounding him with long lance or sword. ¹³And having set foot beside foot, and having fixed shield against shield, and crest on crest, and helmet on helmet, and breast against breast, struggle in fight with his man, having seized either the hilt of his sword, or his long lance. But do ye, ¹⁴O light-armed soldiers, crouching under your shields, some from one quarter, some from another, make them fall with huge stones, and with polished spears, as ye dart at them, and stand near to the ¹⁵heavy-armed troops.
items.coverage_note: Whole 38-line elegy (Tyrtaeus fr. 11 W), same extent as Campbell. Literal prose; Banks prints no Greek. Footnote reference numbers are kept as superscripts, the footnotes omitted; words Banks prints in italics (supplied for sense) appear in plain type. End-of-line hyphenation removed.
items.match_evidence: Since you are the race of unconquered Heracles, take courage; Zeus does not yet turn his neck aside (Campbell 1-2); hold the shield against the foremost, count life hateful and the black fates dear as the sun's rays (4-6); the works of Ares, flight and pursuit (7-10); those who stand together die fewer and save the people behind (11-13); the shame of a corpse wounded in the back (17-20); stand firm, bite the lip, cover thighs, shins, breast and shoulders with the shield, brandish the spear, shake the crest (21-26); foot to foot, shield on shield, crest on crest (31-33); you light-armed, throw great stones and polished javelins (35-38).

items.text: ¹I would neither commemorate, nor hold in account a man, either for excellence in running, or for wrestling; no, nor though he should have the bulk and strength of the Cyclopes, and in speed surpass ²Thracian Boreas. No, nor though he should in personal appearance be more graceful than ³Tithonus, and should be more rich than Midas or ⁴Cinyras. Nor though he should be more kingly than Pelops, son of Tantalus, and have the ⁵soft-voiced tongue of Adrastus; nor yet if he should have all glory, save that of resistless valour; for he is not a man brave in war, ⁶unless he have the courage to face bloody slaughter, and standing near attack the foemen. But this is excellence, this the best prize among men, and noblest for a young man to carry off. And this is a common good to a city, and all its people, namely, whatsoever man standing firm bides unceasingly in the front ranks, and is wholly forgetful of base flight, when he has ⁷staked his life, and enduring spirit; but has the heart to fall, standing beside his next neighbour. This man is good in war. And quickly does he turn in flight the sturdy phalanxes of foemen, and ⁸zealously stem the wave of battle. He too himself having fallen amid the foremost, loses his life, and (at the same time) having brought renown to his city and people and sire: pierced in many places through breast, and round shield, and through his cuirass in the front. Him young alike and old lament, and the whole state is distressed for him with painful regret. His ⁹tomb and children are famous among men, ay, ¹⁰his children's children, and his race after him. Never does his fair fame or his name perish, but though he be on earth, he becomes immortal, whom, bravely bearing himself, standing firm, and fighting for country and for children, impetuous Ares shall have destroyed. But should he have escaped the fate of death that-lays-men-out-at-length; and as victor, have borne off the splendid boast of battle won, all honour him, young and old alike; and ¹¹after tasting many delights, he comes to Hades. Growing old, he is eminent amid the citizens, nor does any one wish to hurt him in point of respect or justice. And all ¹²on the seats, alike young, and those of his age, and they who are still older, give place to him. Let every one now strive in his spirit to reach the summit of ¹³excellence like this, not ¹⁴slackening warfare.

Footnote reference numbers are kept as superscripts, the footnotes omitted; words Banks prints in italics (supplied for sense) appear in plain type. End-of-line hyphenation removed.
items.match_evidence: I would not mention or account a man for speed of foot or wrestling (Campbell 1-2), not if he had the size and strength of the Cyclopes and outran Thracian Boreas (3-4), were more handsome than Tithonus, richer than Midas and Cinyras (5-6), more kingly than Pelops son of Tantalus, with the honey-tongue of Adrastus (7-8), unless he has furious valour and can face bloody slaughter (9-12); this is excellence, the best prize for a young man (13-14); the fallen hero mourned by young and old, his tomb and children's children famous (23-30); the survivor honoured, all give place to him on the seats (35-42); let each strive for this excellence (43-44).

items.edition: The Idylls of Theocritus, Bion, and Moschus, and the War-Songs of Tyrtaeus, literally translated into English prose by the Rev. J. Banks, M.A. (London: Henry G. Bohn, 1853; Bohn's Classical Library)

items.text:
How long lie ye inactive? when will ye have a brave spirit, young men? and are ye not ¹ashamed of the dwellers all around, since ye dally thus exceedingly? For ye think ye ²sit secure in peace, yet war possesses the whole land.
* * * * * *
³And let a man, as he dies, discharge his javelin for the last time. For it is both honourable and noble for a man to fight for land, and children, and wedded wife, with his foes; and death will come at some time, whensoever in truth the fates shall have allotted. But let every one, having lifted aloft his lance, and ⁴gathered up his stout heart under his shield, go right forward, when the battle first is joined. For it is not fated by any means that a man should escape death at least, no, not though he be by family of immortal ancestry. Often ⁵he comes forth, after having escaped battle-strife and din of javelins, and in his home fated death found him. Now the latter is not in like manner a friend ⁶to the commonalty, nor regretted by them, whilst the former, the brave man, small and great bewail, if aught shall have happened to him. For the whole people together regrets a stout-hearted hero, when he dies, and living he is worthy of the demigods. For they behold him with their eyes even as a ⁷tower, since, though single-handed, he performs deeds worth those of many.
items.coverage_note: Banks prints this elegy as Tyrtaeus IV (Stobaeus' lemma was disputed in older editions; it is now assigned to Callinus). Same extent as Campbell: lines 1-4, a row of asterisks marking the lacuna where Campbell prints dots, then lines 5-21. Literal prose; Banks prints no Greek. Footnote reference numbers are kept as superscripts, the footnotes omitted; words Banks prints in italics (supplied for sense) appear in plain type. End-of-line hyphenation removed.
items.match_evidence: How long will you lie idle, young men, when will you have a valiant heart, are you not ashamed before your neighbours (Campbell 1-3)? you think you sit in peace but war holds the whole land (3-4); [lacuna]; let a man hurl his javelin one last time as he dies (5); honourable to fight for land, children and wedded wife (6-7); death comes when the Fates spin it (8-9); go straight forward with spear raised and heart gathered behind the shield (9-11); no man may escape death though of immortal descent (12-13); often one who fled the battle meets death at home (14-15); the whole people mourns a stout-hearted man, they look on him as a tower, alone he does the deeds of many (18-21).

items.citation: Simonides [of Amorgos] fr. 18 Jacobs (i. 128), "The Miseries of Life", Bland (1813) p. 184
items.text:
Jove rules the world, and with resistless sway
Demands to-morrow what he gave to-day;
In vain our thoughts to future scenes we cast,
Or only read them darkly in the past;
For hope enchanting points to new delights,
And charms with dulcet sounds, and heav'nly sights;
Expecting yet some fancied bliss to share,
We grasp at bubbles that dissolve in air,
And some a day, and some whole years await
The whims and chances of capricious fate;
Nor yet the lovely visions are possess'd—
Another year remains to make them blest.
While age creeps on to tear their dreams away,
And grim diseases hover round their prey;
Or war with iron hold unlocks the grave,
Devouring myriads of the young and brave.
Some on the billows rock'd that roll on high
Cling to the plank in vain, and wasted die;
Some by the halter lay their miseries down,
And rush unsummon'd to a place unknown.
Our very sweets possess a secret harm,
Teem with distress, and poison while they charm;
The fatal Sisters hover round our birth,
And dash with bitter dregs our cup on earth:
Yet cease to murmur at thy fate in vain,
And in oblivion steep the shaft of pain.
items.coverage_note: Signed 'B.' (Robert Bland). Free rhymed version of the whole 24-line poem (26 lines); Bland's 'Simonides' is Semonides of Amorgos (Jacobs' numbering i. 128). Same extent as Campbell, rendered loosely. Bland prints no Greek.
items.match_evidence: Zeus holds the end of all things and disposes as he wills (Campbell 1-2); men live like beasts from day to day, not knowing how god will bring each thing to pass, fed by hope (3-7); some wait a day, some years, thinking next year to be rich (7-10); old age, disease, war, death at sea, the noose (11-20); ills without number from the Fates (20-22); if men listened to me we would not love our misfortunes nor torment our hearts (22-24).

items.edition: Collections from the Greek Anthology, and from the Pastoral, Elegiac, and Dramatic Poets of Greece, by the Rev. Robert Bland and others (London, 1813)
items.citation: Simonides fr. 104 Jacobs (i. 145), "Uncertainty of Life", Merivale in Bland (1813) p. 185
items.text:
All human things are subject to decay;
And well the man of Chios tuned his lay,
“Like leaves on trees the race of man is found.”
Yet few receive the melancholy sound,
Or in their breasts imprint this solemn truth;
For hope is near to all, but most to youth.
Hope's vernal season leads the laughing hours,
And strews o'er every path the fairest flowers.
To cloud the scene no distant mists appear,
Age moves no thought, and death awakes no fear.
Ah, how unmindful is the giddy crowd
Of the small span to youth and life allow'd
Ye who reflect, the short-lived good employ,
And while the power remains, indulge your joy.
items.coverage_note: Signed 'M.' (J. H. Merivale) in the 1813 Collections (reprinted 1833). Merivale's first line ('All human things are subject to decay') renders a line that precedes Campbell's text in older editions (οὐδὲν ἐν ἀνθρώποισι μένει χρῆμ' ἔμπεδον αἰεί); the remaining 13 lines render Campbell 1-13. Bland/Merivale print no Greek.
items.match_evidence: The man of Chios said it best: as the generation of leaves, so of men (Campbell 1-2); few who hear it take it to heart, for hope is in every man, rooted in the young (3-5); while a man has the flower of youth he plans much, expects neither old age nor death (6-9); fools, not knowing how short the time of youth and life (10-12); learn this and indulge your soul with good things to the end (12-13).

items.text: but, like a dream, precious youth is a short-lived thing: and presently over-head hangs unhappy and unsightly old age.
items.coverage_note: PARTIAL: Campbell's lines 1-3 (ἀλλ' ὀλιγοχρόνιον ... ὑπερκρέμαται) also stand in the Theognis collection (1020-1022), and Banks's note 5 on p. 272 says these verses 'are the work of Mimnermus'. Only the clause rendering those three lines is given (the preceding Theognidean lines 1017-1019 = Mimnermus 5.1-3 West are not in Campbell's text). Campbell's lines 4-5 (hateful and dishonoured old age that makes a man unknown and harms eyes and mind), preserved only by Stobaeus, are not in Theognis and not translated.
items.match_evidence: Precious youth is short-lived like a dream (Campbell 1-2); painful and ugly old age at once hangs over the head (2-3).
